Did anything change suddenly? ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Reveal the grouped line plot ::: {#68ea2c21 .cell fig-height='5' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} palette = {"Outdoor gear": "#00798c", "Smart home": "#edae49", "Office supplies": "#d1495b"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5)) sns.lineplot(data=visits_long, x="month", y="visits", hue="product_line", palette=palette, marker="o", markersize=4, lw=2, ax=ax) ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp("2025-01-01"), color="gray", ls=":", lw=1.5) ax.text(pd.Timestamp("2025-01-15"), ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.97, "Site redesign", color="gray", va="top") ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator(bymonth=[1, 7])) ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b\n%Y")) ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v/1000:.0f}k")) ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Monthly visits", title="Three product lines, three different stories") ax.legend(title="", loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.14), ncol=3, frameon=False) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](time_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=1322 height=717} ::: ::: [Each line tells a different story, and you can read all three in seconds:]{.reveal-note} - **Outdoor gear** is **seasonal**: it peaks every summer and bottoms out every winter. - **Smart home** is **steadily growing**, more than doubling over three years. - **Office supplies** was flat, then **dropped about 40%** right when the site was redesigned. That's a problem worth investigating. [In the table, the seasonal swing looks like noise, the steady growth is spread across 36 rows, and the drop is just one column of numbers getting a bit smaller partway down.]{.reveal-note} ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Data format for the grouped line plot The table above is **wide** (one column per product line), but `sns.lineplot()` with `hue=` needs **long** data: **one row per product line per month**. Three years of monthly data for three product lines is 36 × 3 = 108 rows in `visits_long`. | Column | Type | Role in the chart | |---|---|---| | `month` | date (`datetime64`, first day of each month) | `x`: the time axis | | `product_line` | text: Outdoor gear, Smart home, Office supplies | `hue`: one line per unique value | | `visits` | integer | `y` | Two details matter: - **`month` must be real dates, not text.** In the wide table it's stored as text like `"2025-01"`. The "Site redesign" marker (`pd.Timestamp("2025-01-01")`) and the date-axis labels (`mdates`) only work on a true date column. Starting from text, convert with `pd.to_datetime()`. - **One row per group per time point.** If a product line had several rows for the same month, `lineplot()` would average them and draw a shaded uncertainty band instead of a single clean line. The keys of the `palette` dictionary must match the `product_line` values exactly. See the note below for converting wide data to long. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Wide vs. long data Spreadsheets usually store time series **wide** (one column per group). `seaborn` wants data **long** (one row per observation, with a column naming the group), which makes `hue=` work. Converting is one line with `pandas`: ::: {#1f3231fe .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} long = visits_wide.melt(id_vars="month", var_name="product_line", value_name="visits") long.head(8) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
